# TexForge

> TexForge is a Windows desktop application for batch image processing and texture atlas packing. It ships 113 batch actions, 69 atlas image formats and 24 engine data formats, with a GUI and a CLI sharing one pipeline. UI is available in Chinese and English. Distributed through Microsoft Store.

## Key facts

- Product: TexForge 1.3.4
- Platform: Windows 10 / Windows 11 (x64)
- Category: Multimedia design / graphics tooling
- Distribution: Microsoft Store — https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9p7wpkn0t5cn?cid=DevShareMCLPCS&hl=zh-CN&gl=HK
- Repository: https://github.com/lijiannan1241/TexForge
- Contact: cdljn2022@gmail.com
- Privacy: runs fully locally; no telemetry, no image uploads, no tracking SDKs
- Pricing: see the Microsoft Store listing for the current price and trial options

## Capabilities

- Batch processing: 113 actions covering resize, crop, rotate, watermark, format conversion, compression, metadata and more
- Texture atlases: packing with padding, extrusion, trimming, rotation and power-of-two validation; 69 descriptor formats
- Engine export: 24 data formats for Unity, Unreal, Godot, Cocos, Phaser, PixiJS, Spine, LibGDX, SpriteKit, Egret, LayaAir, WeChat mini games, plus custom templates
- Game pixel tools: normal map generation, ORM/RMA channel packing, mipmaps, platform size limits, engine folder planning
- Asset audits: naming, dimension, duplicate and missing-pair checks with CSV/JSON reports
- Automation: texforge-cli shares presets with the GUI for scripts and CI

## Workflow

1. Import and scan — Drop folders or individual images into a workspace. TexForge scans subdirectories recursively and filters by extension, naming rules and size range, so you see exactly what is about to be processed.
2. Configure actions and parameters — Stack actions for batch work, or set layout, padding, trimming and target format for atlases. Save the result as a preset (JSON) — the smallest reusable unit a team can share.
3. Preview and validate — See the result before exporting. Atlases show a layout preview and occupancy, batch runs offer a per-image comparison, and constraint checks flag oversized textures, inconsistent padding and empty regions early.
4. Export and report — One run produces images, descriptors and a result report. Atlas image and descriptor share a name and folder, so the engine resolves them immediately; the report records what happened to every image.

## Frequently asked questions

- Q: What is TexForge?
  A: TexForge is a Windows desktop tool that puts batch image processing and texture atlas packing into one pipeline. It ships both a GUI and a CLI, aimed at indie developers, artists and technical artists.
- Q: How is it different from Photoshop actions or ImageMagick scripts?
  A: Photoshop actions live inside one application and ImageMagick means hand-assembling command lines. TexForge makes action sequences, atlas parameters and engine exports configurable, saves them as presets shared by GUI and CLI, and ships atlas descriptors and engine folder planning that generic image tools do not provide.
- Q: Who is it for?
  A: Indie developers, 2D / 2.5D artists, technical artists, outsourcing reviewers and small teams shipping to several platforms.
- Q: Is the UI available in Chinese?
  A: Yes. Pick Chinese or English on first run and switch later in settings; both interfaces expose the same features.
- Q: Which image formats are supported?
  A: Common raster formats can be read and written, including PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, TIFF, TGA and DDS, with optional extended codecs.
- Q: What are the 69 atlas formats?
  A: Descriptor-plus-image combinations for Unity, Godot, Unreal, Cocos2d, Phaser 2/3, PixiJS, Spine, LibGDX, SpriteKit, Starling, Egret, LayaAir and WeChat mini games, plus generic JSON / XML / plist / CSS / CSV.
- Q: Which game engines are supported?
  A: Built-in folder planning and metadata export for Unity, Unreal, Godot and Cocos — 24 engine data formats in total — with custom templates for anything else.
- Q: Can I use custom engine templates?
  A: Yes. Fields and nesting can be trimmed to fit in-house engines and internal conventions.
- Q: Does it support HTML5 runtimes such as WeChat mini games?
  A: Yes. Atlas descriptors and metadata export directly for WeChat mini games, Cocos, Phaser and PixiJS runtimes.
- Q: Does atlas packing support padding, trimming and power-of-two?
  A: Yes. Set padding and edge extrusion, trim by alpha bounds, rotate small sprites, and validate POT / NPOT and maximum size limits.
- Q: Can the normal map Y axis be switched?
  A: Yes. Switch between OpenGL and DirectX conventions, adjust strength, and keep normal maps on the linear data path.
- Q: How do mipmaps and platform size checks work?
  A: Power-of-two mip chains are generated, then validated against mobile and desktop size limits; oversized textures are flagged before export.
- Q: How many images can it process?
  A: There is no hard limit; throughput depends on disk space, memory and image dimensions. For large jobs, validate the preset on a small sample first.
- Q: Where are nine-patch and sprite splitting?
  A: In the Atlas toolbox workspace: split sprite sheets by grid or transparent gutters, or slice nine-patch borders, then feed the output into batch actions or the atlas packer.
- Q: How do I install and update?
  A: Install from Microsoft Store to receive automatic updates. The store listing shows the current version and system requirements.
- Q: What are the system requirements?
  A: Windows 10 / Windows 11 (x64). 8 GB RAM or more is recommended for large batches; disk space depends on the image set.
- Q: Does it need an internet connection?
  A: No. After installation it works offline; all processing happens locally.
- Q: Does it collect my data?
  A: No. TexForge runs entirely on your machine. It does not upload images, send telemetry, or include advertising or tracking SDKs. See the privacy policy for details.
- Q: What is the difference between the GUI and the CLI?
  A: They share the same pipeline and presets. The GUI is for tuning and previewing; the CLI (texforge-cli) is for batch scripts, build servers and CI automation.
- Q: Can it run in CI?
  A: Yes. The CLI reads the same preset files as the GUI, reports success through exit codes, and writes result reports you can archive as build artifacts.
- Q: How do I report a problem?
  A: Email cdljn2022@gmail.com or open an issue on the GitHub repository. Include the version, steps to reproduce and the result report to speed things up.

## Blog posts

- [Batch image processing in practice: configure once, process thousands](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/batch-image-processing-guide.html) (2026-09-02): How to combine TexForge's 113 batch actions into a stable asset pipeline, from action sequences and presets to retrying failed items.
- [A complete guide to texture atlas packing: padding, trimming, POT and 69 formats](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/texture-atlas-packing.html) (2026-09-09): An atlas is more than a big image full of sprites. Padding, extrusion, trimming, rotation and format choice decide runtime sampling quality and memory cost.
- [24 engine data formats: export for Unity, Godot, Unreal and Cocos at once](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/engine-export-formats.html) (2026-09-16): The same atlas needs different descriptors and folder layouts per engine. A look at 24 formats, folder planning and custom templates.
- [Normal maps and channel packing: doing ORM, roughness and metallic right](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/normal-map-channel-packing.html) (2026-09-23): From height maps to normal maps, ORM / RMA channel packing and Y-axis conventions — the color-space and channel-order traps worth avoiding.
- [Mipmaps and platform size limits: stop tripping on mobile textures](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/mipmap-and-platform-limits.html) (2026-09-30): How mip chains affect memory and looks, POT versus NPOT, platform size caps, and how to validate before export.
- [CLI and CI integration: wire your asset pipeline into the build](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/cli-automation-ci.html) (2026-10-07): The GUI and CLI share one pipeline. Use texforge-cli, JSON reports and exit codes to make asset processing a verifiable build step.
- [Sprite sheets and nine-patch: slicing mobile UI the right way](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/sprite-sheet-and-nine-patch.html) (2026-10-14): Sprite splitting, nine-patch stretch regions, batch borders and rounded corners, and verifying shapes in the engine afterwards.
- [EXIF / XMP / IPTC workflows: copyright, authorship and bulk cleanup](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/exif-xmp-iptc-workflow.html) (2026-10-21): How to stamp copyright and authorship consistently, strip private fields before publishing, and handle ICC profiles correctly.
- [Compression and target size: balancing quality against package size](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/compression-and-target-size.html) (2026-10-28): Target-size compression, PNG optimization, lossy versus lossless trade-offs, and verifying results in bulk instead of eyeballing every file.
- [An indie game art pipeline: from source files to a shippable build](https://lijiannan1241.github.io/TexForge/en/blog/indie-game-asset-pipeline.html) (2026-11-11): A small indie project as the running example: folder structure, naming rules, how the four workspaces divide the work, engine integration and a pre-release checklist.
